name: __clear_user
prose: Function __clear_user(to, n), written as one inline-assembly block, that zeroes n bytes of user memory starting at to. The caller must have checked the range with access_ok (stated in the comment above it; the function does not check). It returns the value left in the n register, which the comment describes as the number of bytes not cleared. Behaviour: if to is 0 it jumps to the end and returns n unchanged without writing anything; if n is 0 it returns 0; if to is not 4-byte aligned it clears byte by byte; if to is 4-byte aligned it first clears 32-byte blocks (eight word stores, n reduced by 32 only after the eight stores), then 4-byte words (n reduced by 4 after each store), then the remaining bytes (n reduced by 1 after each store). A fault on any of the user stores is redirected through the exception table to label 9, and n then holds the count as of the last completed block, word or byte step, so it includes any words of the faulting 32-byte block that were already zeroed; if all stores succeed it returns 0 and all n bytes at to are zero.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: the count is decremented only after a whole 32-byte block, word or byte store sequence (usercopy.c slice 8:-16: and the subi after them), so after a fault inside a block the returned n counts words that were already written; the old prose said bytes before the fault are zeroed and the rest are the return value, which is not exact. Not claimed: what the code does after label 9 depends on the condition flag, so the prose only says n is returned as left in the register.

name: cache_wbinv_range
prose: Function cache_wbinv_range(start, end) for the csky v2 cache; it returns nothing. It calls dcache_wb_range(start, end) and then icache_inv_range(start, end). dcache_wb_range rounds start down to an L1_CACHE_BYTES boundary and, for each line address i from there while i < end, issues dcache.cval1 on i (write back the data line), then sync_is(). icache_inv_range depends on the configuration: with CONFIG_CPU_HAS_ICACHE_INS it loops the same way issuing icache.iva per line and then sync_is(), with no lock; without it, it builds a range parameter and, if irqs_disabled() is true, calls local_icache_inv_range directly (only the calling CPU invalidates), otherwise it calls on_each_cpu(local_icache_inv_range, &param, 1) so that every online CPU invalidates and the call waits for completion; local_icache_inv_range takes cache_lock with spin_lock_irqsave while it does the cr22/cr17 line operations for the range, releases it, and calls sync_is(). The loops operate on lines that start at the line containing start and stop when the line address reaches end, so when start is greater than end they do no line operation only if the line address of start is not below end; if start and end fall in the same cache line one line operation is still done.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: start > end can still operate on one line when both are in the same cache line (loop starts at start rounded down, cachev2.c:80-86). Round 1 (lock in fallback) already in the old prose. Round 2 (on_each_cpu when irqs disabled) is wrong against the prose: the old text and the code both call the local function directly when irqs are disabled (cachev2.c:57-63). Slice contained only cache_wbinv_range; callees read in the real file lines 20-93.

name: tcm_setup_pool
prose: Static __init function with no arguments. It computes pool_size and tcm_pool_start from the TCM page counts and the linker symbols (different expressions under CONFIG_HAVE_DTCM), then sets the global tcm_pool to gen_pool_create(2, -1) (minimum allocation order 2, any node) without checking the result for NULL, and calls gen_pool_add(tcm_pool, tcm_pool_start, pool_size, -1). Return paths: (1) if gen_pool_add returns non-zero it prints an error with pr_err and returns that value (gen_pool_add reports -ENOMEM on allocation failure), with tcm_pool already created but without the region; (2) otherwise it prints an info line with the size and start address and returns 0. If gen_pool_create returned NULL, the following gen_pool_add call would use a NULL pool; this function does not handle that case.
note: Contract cleared: it only states result <= 0 (reviewers rounds 1, 2 and 15 all complained) and the function writes a global. Reviewer round 2 (the old text claimed -EINVAL for NULL) is partly right: the code does not check NULL (tcm.c slice 147-149); the old prose already said the NULL return is not checked. Precondition about tcm_mapping_init removed: nothing in this function enforces or uses it.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE0(rt_sigreturn)
prose: Generated syscall function sys_rt_sigreturn (hexagon, no arguments), defined by SYSCALL_DEFINE0(rt_sigreturn). It takes regs = current_pt_regs(), sets current->restart_block.fn = do_no_restart_syscall, and takes frame = the user stack pointer pt_psp(regs) as a struct rt_sigframe pointer. It goes to badframe if access_ok(frame, sizeof(*frame)) fails or if copying the saved signal mask frame->uc.uc_sigmask from user space fails. Otherwise it installs that mask with set_current_blocked (this happens before the register context is restored, so the new mask stays installed on any later failure), then calls restore_sigcontext(regs, &frame->uc.uc_mcontext), which copies the saved registers from user space into regs and returns non-zero on a copy error (regs may already be partly overwritten) and the function then goes to badframe; then sets pt_psp(regs) = regs->r29, sets regs->syscall_nr = -1, and goes to badframe if restore_altstack(&frame->uc.uc_stack) fails (the changes above are not undone). On success it returns regs->r00. At badframe it calls force_sig(SIGSEGV) and returns 0.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: set_current_blocked runs before restore_sigcontext (signal.c:238-241) and nothing undoes it on failure; old prose implied the badframe path restores nothing else. The slice cut the tail; badframe read in the real file (signal.c:253-256). Name is the SYSCALL_DEFINE0 invocation since the generated name sys_rt_sigreturn does not occur literally.

name: ATOMIC_OPS(add, i, add, +)
prose: Generated function arch_atomic_add(int i, atomic_t *v) (static inline, produced by ATOMIC_OP(add, i, add) inside ATOMIC_OPS(add, i, add, +)). It executes a single amadd.w instruction on v->counter with $zero as the destination, so the 32-bit add of i is atomic and the old value is discarded; it is the plain (non-_db, relaxed) form with only the compiler memory clobber, not a full-barrier instruction. It returns nothing and takes no lock or reference.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: ATOMIC_OP emits am#asm_op.w with no _db suffix (loongarch/include/asm/atomic.h:37-45), so old claim of a full-barrier amadd_db.w was wrong; the _db variants are the separate ATOMIC_OP_RETURN/ATOMIC_FETCH_OP instances generated by the same ATOMIC_OPS invocation (not the one described here). Name is the file-level macro invocation (atomic.h:82).

name: __BUILD_CSR_OP(euen)
prose: Generated function set_csr_euen(unsigned long set) (static inline, from __BUILD_CSR_COMMON(csr_euen) via __BUILD_CSR_OP(euen)). It reads the EUEN CSR with read_csr_euen() (a 32-bit csr_read32), computes new = res | set, writes new back with write_csr_euen() (csr_write32, so only the low 32 bits reach the CSR), and returns res, the value read before the write. The read and the write are two separate CSR accesses, so the update is not atomic with respect to interrupts or other writers.
note: Macro-generated (loongarch.h __BUILD_CSR_COMMON at 195-231, instantiated at 235-237); name is the invocation because set_csr_euen does not occur literally. The old prose is accurate; added the 32-bit access width and non-atomicity.

name: init_cpu_fullname
prose: Static __init function with no arguments, registered with arch_initcall. It calls of_property_read_string(of_root, "model", &model). If that returns 0 it makes a copy with kstrdup(model, GFP_KERNEL); if the copy fails it returns -ENOMEM at once, changing nothing. Otherwise it stores strsep(&cpuname, " ") in loongson_sysconf.cpuname: that is the start of the copy, truncated at the first space character (the string is empty if the model starts with a space); the allocation is not freed and stays reachable through loongson_sysconf.cpuname, while any earlier value of that field is overwritten. If of_property_read_string returned non-zero nothing of this is done. In every case that does not return -ENOMEM it then checks loongson_sysconf.cpuname (the new or the pre-existing value): if it is non-NULL and its first 8 characters are "Loongson", it sets __cpu_full_name[cpu] to that pointer for each cpu from 0 to NR_CPUS - 1. It then returns 0. Return values are only -ENOMEM and 0.
note: Reviewer round 15 right on both points: strsep returns the original start of the allocation, so the pointer is kept and nothing is leaked (env.c slice 49-52), and the Loongson check and __cpu_full_name loop (55-58) run even when the model property could not be read, so old text saying nothing changes and 0 is returned was wrong. Round 2 (strsep splits only on a space; allocation leaked) is right about the space and wrong about the leak. Round 1 (side effect on __cpu_full_name) is already in the old prose.

name: pv_send_ipi_mask
prose: Static function taking a cpumask pointer mask and an IPI action number; it returns nothing. It returns at once if mask is empty. If action is ACTION_BOOT_CPU it calls native_ops.send_ipi_mask(mask, action) and returns, setting no message bits and issuing no hypercall. Otherwise action becomes BIT(action) (so the action number must be a valid bit position) and for each CPU i in mask it atomically ORs that bit into the per-CPU irq_stat message word with atomic_fetch_or; if the previous message word was non-zero (any bit, not only this action) the CPU is skipped, the bit having already been ORed in and no hypercall being queued for it. For each other CPU it takes the hardware id cpu = cpu_logical_map(i) and adds it to a 128-bit bitmap (KVM_IPI_CLUSTER_SIZE = 2 * BITS_PER_LONG) based at min: the first CPU sets min = max = cpu; a lower id within the window shifts the bitmap and lowers min, a higher id within the window may raise max; an id outside the window first sends the pending bitmap with kvm_hypercall3(KVM_HCALL_FUNC_IPI, low word, high word, min), then restarts the bitmap at that id; the bit (cpu - min) is then set. After the loop, if the bitmap is non-zero it sends it with one more kvm_hypercall3. It takes no lock; the message-word updates are the only state changes besides the hypercalls.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: the cluster is built from cpu_logical_map(i) (hardware ids), not logical CPU numbers (paravirt.c slice line 96); the old prose said logical numbers. Round 2 (skip when any bit already set) already stated in the old prose; original (ACTION_BOOT_CPU delegates to native_ops) also already stated. Slice 75-122.

name: arch_do_signal_or_restart
prose: Function taking the saved user register context regs of the current task; it returns nothing. It calls get_signal(&ksig). If a signal is pending, it calls handle_signal(&ksig, regs), which sets up the signal frame and may change regs and the blocked-signal mask (it can also restore or change the syscall restart state through the frame setup), and returns immediately. Otherwise: if regs->regs[0] is non-zero (the marker do_syscall sets to the syscall number plus one when the entry came from a system call), then if regs->regs[4] (the syscall result) is -ERESTARTNOHAND, -ERESTARTSYS or -ERESTARTNOINTR it sets regs->regs[4] = regs->orig_a0 (the original value of a0 saved by do_syscall) and decrements regs->csr_era by 4; if it is -ERESTART_RESTARTBLOCK it sets regs->regs[4] = regs->orig_a0, regs->regs[11] = __NR_restart_syscall and decrements regs->csr_era by 4; for any other value of regs->regs[4] it changes none of those; in all cases where regs->regs[0] was non-zero it then sets regs->regs[0] = 0. If regs->regs[0] was zero, regs is not changed. In every no-signal path it finally calls restore_saved_sigmask().
note: Reviewer round 15 right: handle_signal changes regs and the mask, so they are not left untouched. Round 2 right on orig_a0: do_syscall saves the original a0 there (syscall.c:57), it is not the syscall number, and regs[0] holds nr + 1 (54); the clearing of regs[0] for non-restart values was already in the old prose. Original rejection (restore_saved_sigmask on no-signal path) already in the old prose. Slice 8-42.

name: SYSCALL_DEFINE6(mmap, unsigned long, addr, unsigned long, len, unsigned long, prot, unsigned long, flags, unsigned long, fd, unsigned long, offset)
prose: Generated syscall function sys_mmap (loongarch) taking addr, len, prot, flags, fd and offset, defined by SYSCALL_DEFINE6(mmap, ...). If (offset & ~PAGE_MASK) is non-zero, i.e. offset is not a multiple of the page size, it returns -EINVAL and creates no mapping. Otherwise it returns the value of ksys_mmap_pgoff(addr, len, prot, flags, fd, offset >> PAGE_SHIFT) unchanged (a mapped address or a negative error code). There are only these two returns; it takes no lock itself.
note: Macro-generated function; name is the SYSCALL_DEFINE6 invocation (syscall.c:29-36). Old prose is accurate.

name: next_frame
prose: Static function taking an unwind_state pointer state, that advances an unwind to the next frame; info is &state->stack_info. Returns: (1) false at once, with state unchanged, if unwind_done(state) is already true. Otherwise it loops: (a) it calls unwind_by_prologue(state); if that returns true it sets state->pc = unwind_graph_addr(state, state->pc, state->sp) and returns true (state->pc, sp, ra, first and reset are as unwind_by_prologue left them; state->stack_info is not refreshed). (b) If it returned false (possibly after having modified state) and info->type is STACK_TYPE_IRQ and info->end equals state->sp, it reads the pt_regs at info->next_sp: if the regs are from user mode or csr_era is not a kernel text address it leaves the loop to the failure exit; otherwise it sets state->first = true, state->pc = csr_era, state->ra = regs[1], state->sp = regs[3], calls get_stack_info(state->sp, task, info) ignoring its result, and returns true. (c) Otherwise it sets state->sp = info->next_sp and calls get_stack_info on it; get_stack_info returns 0 when the new sp is in a known stack (the loop then repeats from (a)) and a non-zero error (setting info->type to STACK_TYPE_UNKNOWN) when it is not, which leaves the loop. The failure exit sets state->stack_info.type = STACK_TYPE_UNKNOWN and returns false; on that return state may have been altered by earlier unwind_by_prologue calls, and state->sp may have been set to info->next_sp.
note: Reviewer round 15 is wrong: get_stack_info returns 0 on success and -EINVAL on failure (kernel/stacktrace.c, in_task_stack/in_irq_stack paths return 0), so while (!get_stack_info(...)) keeps looping on success and leaves for the false return on failure (unwind_prologue.c slice 224-228). Rounds 1 and 2 (success path does not refresh ra/stack_info; state may be modified before a failed prologue unwind) are already stated and kept. Old prose accurate; restructured into steps.

name: XOR_FUNC_NAME(2)
prose: Generated function __xor_lsx_2(bytes, v1, v2), the body of XOR_FUNC_NAME(2) in xor_template.c instantiated with the lsx macros in xor_simd.c (compiled only when the matching CONFIG_CPU_HAS_ option is set); it returns nothing. It sets lines = bytes / 64 and then runs a do-while loop that always executes its body at least once: per 64-byte line: four 16-byte vld loads of v1 into vector registers 0-3, then for each source four vld loads into registers 4-7 each followed by four vxor.v into registers 0-3, then four vst stores of registers 0-3 back to v1; after each pass it advances v1 and every source pointer by 64 bytes and repeats while --lines is greater than zero. The effect on the processed bytes is v1[j] = v1[j] XOR (the same-position data of each of the 1 source buffers); the sources are only read. It does not enable the vector unit itself (the xor_lsx_2 glue function does). Because the loop is a do-while on an unsigned count, bytes below 64 is not handled correctly (lines is 0, one pass runs and the count then wraps, so the loop would run far past the buffers), and bytes that is not a multiple of 64 leaves the trailing bytes % 64 bytes unprocessed. The buffers must be valid for at least the processed 64-byte lines.
note: Macro-instantiated function: the name __xor_lsx_2 does not occur literally (xor_simd.c:47 defines XOR_FUNC_NAME, xor_template.c defines the bodies), so name is the macro invocation. Old prose omitted the 64-byte granularity, the at-least-one-pass behaviour and the bytes < 64 hazard.

name: atari_tt_hwclk
prose: Function atari_tt_hwclk(op, t) that reads (op == 0) or writes (op != 0) the Atari TT real-time clock using struct rtc_time *t; it returns 0 at its single return statement in all cases. It reads RTC_CONTROL into ctrl first. For a write (op != 0) it prepares values from t: sec, min, hour, day, mon = tm_mon + 1, year = tm_year - atari_rtc_year_offset, wday = tm_wday + (tm_wday >= 0); if ctrl has RTC_24H clear, hour > 11 sets pm = 0x80 and, unless hour is 12, subtracts 12, while hour 0 becomes 12; if ctrl has RTC_DM_BINARY clear it converts the values with bin2bcd (wday only if it is non-negative). Then, for both directions, it polls RTC_FREQ_SELECT until RTC_UIP is clear, using mdelay(1) between polls if in_atomic() or irqs_disabled() and schedule_timeout_interruptible(HWCLK_POLL_INTERVAL) otherwise. Then with interrupts saved and disabled (local_irq_save) it writes RTC_CONTROL = ctrl | RTC_SET; on read it reads the seconds, minutes, hours, day, month, year and day-of-week registers; on write it writes seconds, minutes, hours as hour + pm, day, month, year and, only if wday >= 0, day-of-week; it then writes RTC_CONTROL = ctrl & ~RTC_SET and restores interrupts. For a read it then post-processes: bit 0x80 of the hours value is stripped and sets pm = 1; if ctrl has RTC_DM_BINARY clear all values are converted with bcd2bin; if ctrl has RTC_24H clear then hour 12 with pm clear becomes 0 and pm set with hour other than 12 adds 12; finally it stores tm_sec, tm_min, tm_hour, tm_mday, tm_mon = mon - 1, tm_year = year + atari_rtc_year_offset and tm_wday = wday - 1 in *t. A write does not modify *t.
note: The listed name atari_rtc_get_or_set_time does not occur in the source; slice cut the head and the function is atari_tt_hwclk (atari/time.c:~215-321). Fixed under the real name. Old prose omitted the write-path value preparation (12/24 hour handling and BCD conversion) which happens before the UIP wait; the remaining claims were checked against the slice and kept.

name: ffs
prose: Static inline function ffs(x), the definition used on ColdFire parts with the bitrev instruction (it sits inside the branch guarded by __mcfisaaplus__ or __mcfisac__ and not CONFIG_M68000; other configurations use the generic ffs). If x is 0 it returns 0. Otherwise it returns __ffs(x) + 1, where __ffs executes bitrev followed by ff1 and so yields the zero-based index of the lowest set bit of x; the result is therefore in 1 to 32, for example 17 for x = 65536 and 32 only for x = INT_MIN. It has no side effects and reads no memory (declared __attribute_const__).
note: Contract left empty. The previous contract failed random testing (x=65536 gave result 18) but by the source the value is 17: bitrev then ff1 gives 16 for x = 65536 and the function adds 1 (bitops.h slice 250-255, __ffs just above). The test harness result cannot be reproduced from this code, so no contract is asserted.

name: flush_tlb_all
prose: Sun3 definition of flush_tlb_all (no arguments, returns nothing). It saves the MMU context with sun3_get_context. For each address from 0 up to TASK_SIZE in steps of SUN3_PMEG_SIZE and for each context 0 to 7 it selects that context with sun3_put_context and sets the segmap entry for the address to SUN3_INVALID_PMEG. It then restores the saved context with sun3_put_context. Finally, for each PMEG index from 0 up to but not including SUN3_INVALID_PMEG, if pmeg_alloc[index] is exactly 1 it sets pmeg_alloc[index], pmeg_ctx[index] and pmeg_vaddr[index] to 0. PMEGs whose pmeg_alloc value is not 1 are not touched.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: only PMEG indices below SUN3_INVALID_PMEG with pmeg_alloc == 1 are freed, not every allocated PMEG (tlbflush.h:~110-130). This is the variant in the Sun3 branch; the slice does not contain it, read from the real file. The name suffix in the packet is not part of the function name.

name: flush_tlb_kernel_range
prose: Sun3 definition of flush_tlb_kernel_range(start, end): its only statement is a call to flush_tlb_all(); start and end are not used and it returns nothing. The effect is that of the Sun3 flush_tlb_all: user segmap entries for addresses below TASK_SIZE are set to SUN3_INVALID_PMEG in all 8 contexts, the original context is restored, and the PMEGs with index below SUN3_INVALID_PMEG whose pmeg_alloc is 1 have their pmeg_alloc, pmeg_ctx and pmeg_vaddr cleared. Kernel-range segmap entries are not touched.
note: Reviewer round 15 right: it inherits the limited PMEG freeing of the Sun3 flush_tlb_all, so not every allocated PMEG is freed. Sun3 variant at tlbflush.h:~203-207 in the real file (also present in the 68k-MMU branch with the same body, slice 97-100).

name: flush_tlb_all
prose: Definition of flush_tlb_all for configurations without CONFIG_MMU: its entire body is a single BUG() call, with no arguments, no return value and no other statements. What happens when BUG() runs depends on the configuration (normally the kernel reports a bug and the calling context does not continue).
note: Reviewer round 15 is not about this function: its PMEG remark describes the Sun3 flush_tlb_all, while this body is just BUG() (tlbflush.h, !MMU branch). Old claim that it never returns normally is weakened because BUG() behaviour is configuration dependent.
